title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 106 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 549–551 (Night 106, continuing directly from nights-105), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 106 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. Ḍawʾ al-Makān rejoices at the birth of his son Kān Mā Kān, then has tents pitched over Sharrukān's grave and the Qurʾan recited there through the night. At the graveside the sultan, the vizier Dandān and one of Sharrukān's boon companions each mourn him in verse, the last in a five-line stanza form. Days of war councils follow; weighed down by grief, Ḍawʾ al-Makān asks for stories, and Dandān, who spent the old king's lifetime among tales and poems, promises him that night a story of a lover and his beloved. The commanders gather by candlelight to hear it. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّادِسَةُ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sādisatu baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the sixth after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and sixth night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْمَلِكَ ضَوْءَ الْمَكَانِ لَمَّا أَتَاةُ الْخَبَرُ بِأَنَّ زَوْجَتَهُ وَلَدَتْ وَلَدًا ذَكَرًا فَرِحَ فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-malika ḍawʾa al-makāni lammā atāhu al-khabaru bi-anna zawjatahu waladat waladan dhakaran fariḥa faraḥan shadīdan
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that King Ḍawʾ al-Makān, when the news came to him that his wife had borne a child, a male, rejoiced a rejoicing intense.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the news came to King Ḍawʾ al-Makān that his wife had borne a son, he rejoiced greatly.
sentences.n: The print spells atāhu, “came to him”, with ة for the pronoun ه, as it often does. fariḥa faraḥan shadīdan repeats the verb’s own noun for emphasis: “rejoiced a great rejoicing”.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ الْآنَ اشْتَدَّ ظَهْرِي حَيْثُ رُزِقْتُ وَلَدًا اسْمُهُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla al-āna ishtadda ẓahrī ḥaythu ruziqtu waladan ismuhu kāna mā kāna
sentences.l: And he said: Now my back has grown-strong, since I have been granted a boy whose name is Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.i: And he said, “Now my back is strong again, for I have been granted a son, and his name is Kān Mā Kān.”
sentences.n: The print has حيت, a misprint for حيث (ḥaythu, “since”), corrected here. Shahrazād takes up the night with the words that closed the last one. The child’s name, Kān Mā Kān, means “What was, was”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ لِلْوَزِيرِ دَنْدَانَ إِنِّي أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَتْرُكَ هَذَا الْحُزْنَ وَأَعْمَلَ لِأَخِي خَتْمَاتٍ وَأُمُورًا مِنَ الْخَيْرَاتِ
sentences.tr: thumma qāla li-al-wazīri dandāna innī urīdu an atruka hādhā al-ḥuzna wa-aʿmala li-akhī khatmātin wa-umūran mina al-khayrāti
sentences.l: Then he said to the vizier Dandān: I want to leave this grief, and to do for my brother complete-readings and matters of the good-works.
sentences.i: Then he said to the vizier Dandān, “I mean to put aside this grief, and to have the Qurʾan recited through for my brother, many times over, and other pious works done for him.”
sentences.n: The print has خمات, a misprint for ختمات (khatmāt, complete recitations of the Qurʾan), corrected here; the next sentences show the readers at work by the grave. A khatma is one reading of the whole Qurʾan from beginning to end, often offered for the soul of the dead.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْوَزِيرُ نِعْمَ مَا أَرَدْتَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-wazīru niʿma mā aradta
sentences.l: And the vizier said: Excellent is what you have wished.
sentences.i: “What you intend is excellent,” said the vizier.
sentences.n: niʿma mā, “how good is what …”, is the old verb of praise; the print itself points its first letter.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَمَرَ بِنَصْبِ الْخِيَامِ عَلَى قَبْرِ أَخِيهِ فَنَصَبُوهَا وَجَمَعُوا مِنَ الْعَسْكَرِ مَنْ يَقْرَأُ الْقُرْآنَ فَصَارَ بَعْضُهُمْ يَقْرَأُ وَبَعْضُهُمْ يَذْكُرُ اللَّهَ إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ
sentences.tr: thumma amara bi-naṣbi al-khiyāmi ʿalā qabri akhīhi fa-naṣabūhā wa-jamaʿū mina al-ʿaskari man yaqraʾu al-qurʾāna fa-ṣāra baʿḍuhum yaqraʾu wa-baʿḍuhum yadhkuru allāha ilā al-ṣabāḥi
sentences.l: Then he ordered the pitching of the tents over the grave of his brother, and they pitched them; and they gathered from the army whoever reads the Qurʾan, and some of them began reciting and some of them making-mention of God until the morning.
sentences.i: Then he ordered tents to be pitched over his brother’s grave, and they pitched them; and they gathered from the army all who could recite the Qurʾan, and some recited while others called God to mind until morning.
sentences.n: yadhkuru allāh, “makes mention of God”, is dhikr, the repeated invocation of God’s names. ṣāra with an imperfect verb means “began to, set about”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَقَدَّمَ السُّلْطَانُ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ إِلَى قَبْرِ أَخِيهِ شَرْكَانَ وَسَكَبَ الْعَبَرَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَ هَذِةِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: thumma taqaddama al-sulṭānu ḍawʾu al-makāni ilā qabri akhīhi sharrukāna wa-sakaba al-ʿabarāti wa-anshada hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: Then the sultan Ḍawʾ al-Makān went-forward to the grave of his brother Sharrukān, and poured out the tears, and recited these verses:
sentences.i: Then Sultan Ḍawʾ al-Makān came forward to the grave of his brother Sharrukān, and wept, and recited these lines:
sentences.n: hādhihi, “these”, is printed with ة for ه, a habit of this edition.

sentences.t:
خَرَجُوْا بِهِ وَلِكُلِّ بَاكٍ خَلْفَهُ * صَعَقَاتُ مُوْسَى يَوْمَ دَكِّ الطُّوْرِ
حَتَّى اَتَوْا جَدَثًا كَاَنَّ ضَرِيْحَهُ * فِي قَلْبِ كُلِّ مُوَحِّدٍ مَحْفُوْرُ
مَا كُنْتُ آمُلُ قَبْلَ نَعْشِكَ اَنْ اَرَى * رَضْوَى عَلَى اَيْدِى الرِّجَالِ تَسِيْرُ
كَلَّا وَلَا مِنْ قَبْلِ دَفْنِكَ فِى الثَّرَى * اَنَّ الْكَوَاكِبَ فِى التُّرَابِ تَغُوْرُ
اَمُجَاوِرَ الدَّيْمَاسِ رَهْنُ قَرَارَةٍ * فِيْهَا الضِّيَاءُ بِوَجْهِهِ وَالنُّوْرُ
كَفَلَ الثَّنَاءُ لَهُ بِرَدِّ حَيَاتِهِ * لَمَّا انْطَوَى فَكَانَّهُ مَنْشُورُ
sentences.tr:
kharajū bihi wa-li-kulli bākin khalfahu * ṣaʿaqātu mūsā yawma dakki al-ṭūri
ḥattā ataw jadathan kaʾanna ḍarīḥahu * fī qalbi kulli muwaḥḥidin maḥfūru
mā kuntu āmulu qabla naʿshika an arā * raḍwā ʿalā aydī al-rijāli tasīru
kallā wa-lā min qabli dafnika fī al-tharā * anna al-kawākiba fī al-turābi taghūru
a-mujāwira al-daymāsi rahnu qarāratin * fīhā al-ḍiyāʾu bi-wajhihi wa-al-nūru
kafala al-thanāʾu lahu bi-raddi ḥayātihi * lammā inṭawā fa-kaʾannahu manshūru
sentences.l:
They went out with him, and to every weeper behind him (belonged) the swoonings of Moses on the day of the shattering of the Mount,
until they came to a tomb — as if its grave-trench were dug in the heart of every one-who-confesses-God's-oneness.
I did not hope, before your bier, that I would see Raḍwā upon the hands of the men, moving;
no, nor before your burial in the soil, that the stars would sink into the dust.
O neighbour of the dungeon — a pledge of a low-ground in which (is) the radiance by his face, and the light —
praise has guaranteed to him the giving-back of his life: when he was folded-up, then it is as if he were spread-out.
sentences.i:
They carried him out, and every mourner behind him fell swooning, as Moses fell the day the Mount was shattered,
till they came to a tomb whose grave seemed dug in the heart of every believer.
Before your bier I never thought to see Mount Raḍwā borne along on the hands of men;
no, nor before your burial in the earth, that the stars could set into the dust.
O dweller in the dark vault, held fast in a hollow where his face is the radiance and the light,
praise has pledged to give him back his life: folded away, he is as if unrolled again.
sentences.n: The verse is pointed as printed. Line 1 recalls Qurʾan 7:143, where the mountain crumbles before God and Moses falls senseless (ṣaʿiqa). Raḍwā is a great mountain range in the Hijaz, near Yanbuʿ, west of Medina, a byword for weight: the dead man on his bier is a mountain carried by men. In the last line the rhyme plays on manshūr, “unrolled”, which also means “raised from the dead” (nushūr is the resurrection): the praise spread abroad of him gives him a second life. The print leaves the hamza off fa-kaʾannahu. The fifth line is compressed and its grammar uncertain; the translation follows the likeliest sense, the dead man pledged (rahn) to his low grave, which his face lights.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ مِنْ شِعْرِةِ بَكَى وَبَكَى مَعَهُ جَمِيعُ النَّاسِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha ḍawʾu al-makāni min shiʿrihi bakā wa-bakā maʿahu jamīʿu al-nāsi
sentences.l: And when Ḍawʾ al-Makān finished from his poetry, he wept, and there wept with him all the people.
sentences.i: When Ḍawʾ al-Makān had finished his verses he wept, and all the people wept with him.
sentences.n: shiʿrihi, “his poetry”, again with ة for the pronoun ه.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَتَى إِلَى الْقَبْرِ وَرَمَى نَفْسَهُ عَلَيْهِ وَهُوَ حَائِرٌ وَأَنْشَدَ الْوَزِيرُ قَوْلَ الشَّاعِرِ
sentences.tr: thumma atā ilā al-qabri wa-ramā nafsahu ʿalayhi wa-huwa ḥāʾirun wa-anshada al-wazīru qawla al-shāʿiri
sentences.l: Then he came to the grave and threw himself upon it, he being bewildered; and the vizier recited the saying of the poet:
sentences.i: Then he went to the grave and threw himself on it, beside himself; and the vizier recited the poet’s lines:

sentences.t:
تَرَكْتَ الَّذِي يَفْنِي نِلْتَ الَّذِي يَبْقَى * وَمِثْلُكَ اَقْوَامٌ فَقَدْ سَبَقُوا سَبْقَا
وَفَارَقْتَ هَذِى الدَّارَ مِنْ غَيْرِ رِيبَةٍ * وَعَنْ هَذِهِ الدُّنْيَا تَسُرُّ بِمَا تَلَاقَى
وَكُنْتَ مِنَ الاَعْدَاءِ تُبْدِي وِقَايَةً * اِذَا مَا سِهَامُ الْحَرْبِ سَاوَتِ الرَّشْقَى
اَرَى هَذِهِ الدُّنْيَا غُرُورًا وَبَاطِلًا * وَجَلُّ مُرَادِ الْخَلْقِ اَنْ يَطْلُبُوا الْحَقَّ
حَبَاكَ اِلَهُ الْعَرْشِ فَوْزًا بِجَنَّةٍ * وَاَسْكَنَكَ الْهَادِي بِمَا تَفْعَلُ اَصْدَقَا
وَاِنِّي وَقَدْ اَمْسَيْتُ فِيكَ بِحَسْرَةٍ * اَرَى الْغَرْبَ مَحْزُونًا بِفَقْدِكَ وَالشَّرْقَ
sentences.tr:
tarakta alladhī yafnī nilta alladhī yabqā * wa-mithluka aqwāmun fa-qad sabaqū sabqā
wa-fāraqta hādhī al-dāra min ghayri rībatin * wa-ʿan hādhihi al-dunyā tasurru bi-mā talāqā
wa-kunta mina al-aʿdāʾi tubdī wiqāyatan * idhā mā sihāmu al-ḥarbi sāwati al-rashqā
arā hādhihi al-dunyā ghurūran wa-bāṭilan * wa-jallu murādi al-khalqi an yaṭlubū al-ḥaqqa
ḥabāka ilāhu al-ʿarshi fawzan bi-jannatin * wa-askanaka al-hādī bi-mā tafʿalu aṣdaqā
wa-innī wa-qad amsaytu fīka bi-ḥasratin * arā al-gharba maḥzūnan bi-faqdika wa-al-sharqa
sentences.l:
You left that-which perishes, you gained that-which remains; and (many) like you, peoples — they have gone-before, a going-before.
And you parted from this abode without a doubt, and from this world, glad at what you meet.
And you were, from the enemies, showing a shielding, whenever the arrows of war matched the volley.
I see this world (as) delusion and vanity, and the greater-part of the wish of creatures is that they seek the truth.
The God of the Throne has granted you a triumph with a garden, and the Guide has made you dwell, for what you do, most-true.
And I — and I have come-to-evening over you in regret — I see the west grieving at the loss of you, and the east.
sentences.i:
You have left what perishes and won what endures; and many like you have gone on before.
You have parted from this house without misgiving, and leave this world glad of what you go to meet.
Against the enemy you were a shield whenever the arrows of war flew thick.
I see this world as a cheat and a vanity; the chief thing men should wish is to seek the truth.
The Lord of the Throne has given you the triumph of Paradise, and the Guide has housed you, for your deeds, in the truest place.
And I, left in grief for you, see the West mourning your loss, and the East.
sentences.n: The print has نركت, a misprint for تركت (tarakta, “you left”), corrected here. The verse is otherwise pointed as printed. Metre and sense both want wa-, “and”, before nilta, “you gained”, which the print does not have; it is not added. The rhymes in -qā are loose (al-ḥaqqa and al-sharqa do not carry the long ā), and several phrases are obscure as printed: tasurru bi-mā talāqā, “glad of what you meet”, sāwati al-rashqā, “matched the volley”, and aṣdaqā at the end of the fifth line, here taken as “the truest (abode)”. The translation follows the likeliest sense of each and should be read as tentative there. The print points yafnī (from fanā, yafnī, a by-form of faniya, yafnā). tasurru as pointed is active, “you gladden”; “glad” supposes tusarru.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ الْوَزِيرُ دَنْدَانُ مِنْ شِعْرِةِ بَكَى بُكَاءً شَدِيدًا وَنَثَرَتْ عُيُونُهُ الدُّمُوعَ دُرًّا نَضِيدًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha al-wazīru dandānu min shiʿrihi bakā bukāʾan shadīdan wa-natharat ʿuyūnuhu al-dumūʿa durran naḍīdan
sentences.l: And when the vizier Dandān finished from his poetry, he wept a weeping intense, and his eyes scattered the tears (as) pearls strung-in-order.
sentences.i: When the vizier Dandān had finished his verses he wept bitterly, and his eyes scattered tears like strings of pearls.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: shadīdā / naḍīdā. durr naḍīd, “pearls set in order”, is the stock image for falling tears.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَقَدَّمَ رَجُلٌ كَانَ مِنْ نُدَمَاءِ شَرْكَانَ وَبَكَى حَتَّى حَكَتْ دُمُوعُهُ الْخُلْجَانَ وَذَكَرَ مَا لِشَرْكَانَ مِنَ الْمَكْرُمَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَ شِعْرًا مُخَمَّسًا
sentences.tr: thumma taqaddama rajulun kāna min nudamāʾi sharrukāna wa-bakā ḥattā ḥakat dumūʿuhu al-khuljāna wa-dhakara mā li-sharrukāna mina al-makrumāti wa-anshada shiʿran mukhammasan
sentences.l: Then there came forward a man who was of the boon-companions of Sharrukān, and he wept until his tears resembled the channels; and he made mention of what (belonged) to Sharrukān of the noble-deeds, and recited a poetry five-fold:
sentences.i: Then one of Sharrukān’s boon companions came forward and wept till his tears ran like streams; he spoke of all Sharrukān’s noble deeds, and recited a poem in five-line stanzas:
sentences.n: ḥakat, “resembled”: ḥakā is “to tell” and also “to imitate, be like”. A mukhammas (“made fivefold”) is a poem in stanzas of five half-lines: the first four share a rhyme of their own, and the fifth returns to a rhyme held through the whole poem. Often a poet builds one on an existing poem, adding three half-lines to each of its lines.

sentences.t:
اَيْنَ الْعَطَاءُ وَكَفُّ جُودِكَ فِي الثَّرَى * وَالْجِسْمُ بَعْدَكَ بِالسَّقَامِ قَدِ انْبَرَى
يَا حَادِيَ الْاَضْعَانِ سَرَّكَ مَا تَرَى * كَتَبَتْ دُمُوعِي فَوْقَ خَدِّي اَسْطُرَا
تَعْنِي بِهَا وَتَلَذُّ مِنْهَا مَنْظَرَا
وَاللّٰهِ مَا حَدَّثْتُ عَنْكَ ضَمَائِرِي * كَلَّا وَلَا خَطَرَتْ عُلَاكَ بِخَاطِرِي
اِلَّا وَقَدْ جَرَحَ الدُّمُوعُ مَحَاجِرِي * وَاِذَا صَرَفْتُ اِلَى سِوَاكَ نَوَاظِرِي
جَذَبَ الْغَرَامُ عَنَانَ طَرْفِي فِى الْكَرَي
sentences.tr:
ayna al-ʿaṭāʾu wa-kaffu jūdika fī al-tharā * wa-al-jismu baʿdaka bi-al-saqāmi qadi inbarā
yā ḥādiya al-aḍʿāni sarraka mā tarā * katabat dumūʿī fawqa khaddī asṭurā
taʿnī bihā wa-taladhdhu minhā manẓarā
wa-allāhi mā ḥaddathtu ʿanka ḍamāʾirī * kallā wa-lā kharatat ʿulāka bi-khāṭirī
illā wa-qad jaraḥa al-dumūʿu maḥājirī * wa-idhā ṣaraftu ilā siwāka nawāẓirī
jadhaba al-gharāmu ʿināna ṭarfī fī al-karā
sentences.l:
Where is the giving — and the palm of your bounty (is) in the soil — and the body after you with the sickness has been pared-thin?
O driver of the litter-camels, may what you see gladden you: my tears have written over my cheek lines,
you are concerned with them, and you take-pleasure from them (as) a sight.
By God, I have not spoken of you (to) my inmost-thoughts, no, nor has your loftiness passed through my mind,
but that the tears had wounded my eye-sockets; and when I turn toward other-than-you my glances,
longing pulls the rein of my eye in sleep.
sentences.i:
Where is the giving now, with your open hand in the earth, and my body, since you went, worn thin with sickness?
O driver of the camel-litters, may what you see please you: my tears have written lines down my cheek,
lines for you to dwell on, a sight for you to relish.
By God, never have I spoken of you to my inmost heart, never has your greatness crossed my mind,
without my tears wounding the hollows of my eyes; and when I turn my eyes to anything but you,
longing tugs at the rein of my glance, even in sleep.
sentences.n: The verse is pointed as printed: two stanzas of a mukhammas, the first all in -rā, the second in -rī, closing on the poem’s -rā. al-aḍʿān is printed with ض for ظ: the ẓaʿāʾin are the camel-litters of a departing tribe, the oldest scene of parting in Arabic poetry. taʿnī bihā is obscure as printed (ʿanā, yaʿnī is “to mean”; “to be concerned with” would be taʿnā or tuʿnā); it is read here as “you concern yourself with them”. jaraḥa al-dumūʿu, “the tears wounded”, has a masculine verb before a broken plural, which is regular.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ الرَّجُلُ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ بَكَى ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ هُوَ وَالْوَزِيرُ دَنْدَانُ وَضَجَّ جَمِيعُ الْعَسْكَرِ بِالْبُكَاءِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha al-rajulu min shiʿrihi bakā ḍawʾu al-makāni huwa wa-al-wazīru dandānu wa-ḍajja jamīʿu al-ʿaskari bi-al-bukāʾi
sentences.l: And when the man finished from his poetry, Ḍawʾ al-Makān wept, he and the vizier Dandān, and the whole army clamoured with the weeping.
sentences.i: When the man had finished his poem, Ḍawʾ al-Makān and the vizier Dandān both wept, and the whole army broke into loud weeping.
sentences.n: huwa wa-al-wazīr, “he and the vizier”: the pronoun is repeated so that a second subject can be joined to the first.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمُ انْصَرَفُوا إِلَى الْخِيَامِ وَأَقْبَلَ السُّلْطَانُ عَلَى الْوَزِيرِ دَنْدَانَ وَأَخَذَا يَتَشَاوَرَانِ فِي أَمْرِ الْقِتَالِ وَاسْتَمَرَّا عَلَى ذَلِكَ أَيَّامًا وَلَيَالِيَ
sentences.tr: thumma innahumu inṣarafū ilā al-khiyāmi wa-aqbala al-sulṭānu ʿalā al-wazīri dandāna wa-akhadhā yatashāwarāni fī amri al-qitāli wa-istamarrā ʿalā dhālika ayyāman wa-layāliya
sentences.l: Then they went-off to the tents; and the sultan turned toward the vizier Dandān, and the two began consulting-together in the matter of the fighting, and the two continued at that days and nights.
sentences.i: Then they went back to the tents; and the sultan turned to the vizier Dandān, and the two of them took counsel together about the war, and kept at it for days and nights.
sentences.n: akhadhā yatashāwarāni, “the two began to consult each other”: the verbs are dual. aqbala ʿalā is “to turn one’s attention to” someone.

sentences.t: وَضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ يَتَضَجَّرُ مِنَ الْهَمِّ وَالْأَحْزَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-ḍawʾu al-makāni yataḍajjaru mina al-hammi wa-al-aḥzāni
sentences.l: And Ḍawʾ al-Makān was chafing from the care and the griefs.
sentences.i: And all the while Ḍawʾ al-Makān chafed under his cares and sorrows.
sentences.n: A circumstantial clause with wa-: “while Ḍawʾ al-Makān …”. The rhyme falls on al-makān / al-aḥzān.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ إِنِّي أَشْتَهِي سَمَاعَ أَخْبَارِ النَّاسِ وَأَحَادِيثِ الْمُلُوكِ وَحِكَايَاتِ الْمُتَيَّمِينَ لَعَلَّ اللَّهَ يُفَرِّجُ مَا بِقَلْبِي مِنَ الْهَمِّ الشَّدِيدِ وَيُذْهِبُ عَنِّى الْبُكَاءَ وَالْعَدِيدَ
sentences.tr: thumma qāla innī ashtahī samāʿa akhbāri al-nāsi wa-aḥādīthi al-mulūki wa-ḥikāyāti al-mutayyamīna laʿalla allāha yufarriju mā bi-qalbī mina al-hammi al-shadīdi wa-yudhhibu ʿannī al-bukāʾa wa-al-ʿadīda
sentences.l: Then he said: I desire the hearing of the reports of the people, and the talks of the kings, and the tales of the love-enslaved; perhaps God will relieve what is in my heart of the heavy care, and take away from me the weeping and the wailing.
sentences.i: Then he said, “I long to hear stories of men, tales of kings, and the histories of those enslaved by love; perhaps God will lift the heavy care from my heart and take the weeping and wailing from me.”
sentences.n: al-mutayyamīn, “the love-enslaved”: mutayyam is one made a slave (taym) by love. al-ʿadīd is the wailing of mourners as they count over the virtues of the dead; it rhymes with al-shadīd. ʿannī is printed with ى for ي.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْوَزِيرُ إِنْ كَانَ مَا يُفَرِّجُ هَمَّكَ إِلَّا سَمَاعُ قِصَصِ الْمُلُوكِ مِنْ نَوَادِرِ الْأَخْبَارِ وَحِكَايَاتِ الْمُتَقَدِّمِينَ مِنَ الْمُتَيَّمِينَ وَغَيْرِهِمْ فَإِنَّ هَذَا أَمْرٌ سَهْلٌ لِأَنَّنِي لَمْ يَكُنْ لِي شُغْلٌ فِي حَيَاةِ الْمَرْحُومِ وَالِدِكَ إِلَّا بِالْحِكَايَاتِ وَالْأَشْعَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-wazīru in kāna mā yufarriju hammaka illā samāʿu qiṣaṣi al-mulūki min nawādiri al-akhbāri wa-ḥikāyāti al-mutaqaddimīna mina al-mutayyamīna wa-ghayrihim fa-inna hādhā amrun sahlun li-annanī lam yakun lī shughlun fī ḥayāti al-marḥūmi wālidika illā bi-al-ḥikāyāti wa-al-ashʿāri
sentences.l: And the vizier said: If it is (that) nothing relieves your care except the hearing of the stories of the kings, of the rarities of the reports, and the tales of the former-ones of the love-enslaved and others, then this is an easy matter; because I had no occupation in the life of the late (one) your father except with the tales and the poems.
sentences.i: The vizier said, “If nothing will lift your care but hearing the stories of kings, rare and curious histories, and the tales of lovers and others of old, that is an easy matter; for in the lifetime of your late father I had no other occupation than tales and poems.
sentences.n: in kāna mā … illā, “if it is that nothing … but”: the negative mā with illā limits the subject to one thing. lam yakun lī shughlun, “I had no occupation”, with lam giving the past. al-marḥūm, “the one (God has) had mercy on”, is the usual word for the late, the departed.

sentences.t: وَفِي هَذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ أُحَدِّثُكَ بِخَبَرِ الْعَاشِقِ وَالْمَعْشُوقِ لِأَجْلِ أَنْ يَنْشَرِحَ صَدْرُكَ
sentences.tr: wa-fī hādhihi al-laylati uḥaddithuka bi-khabari al-ʿāshiqi wa-al-maʿshūqi li-ajli an yanshariḥa ṣadruka
sentences.l: And in this night I will tell you the story of the lover and the beloved, for the sake that your breast may open-wide.
sentences.i: Tonight I will tell you the story of a lover and his beloved, so that your heart may be lightened.”
sentences.n: inshirāḥ al-ṣadr, “the widening of the breast”, is relief and good cheer; the image goes back to Qurʾan 94:1, “Did We not widen your breast for you?”. ḥaddatha takes bi- for the thing told: “tell (someone) of”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ كَلَامَ الْوَزِيرِ دَنْدَانَ تَعَلَّقَ قَلْبُهُ بِمَا وَعَدَهُ بِهِ وَلَمْ يَبْقَ لَهُ اشْتِغَالٌ إِلَّا بِانْتِظَارِ مَجِيءِ اللَّيْلِ لِأَجْلِ أَنْ يَسْمَعَ مَا يَحْكِيهِ الْوَزِيرُ دَنْدَانُ مِنْ أَخْبَارِ الْمُتَقَدِّمِينَ مِنَ الْمُلُوكِ وَالْمُتَيَّمِينَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa ḍawʾu al-makāni kalāma al-wazīri dandāna taʿallaqa qalbuhu bi-mā waʿadahu bihi wa-lam yabqa lahu ishtighālun illā bi-intiẓāri majīʾi al-layli li-ajli an yasmaʿa mā yaḥkīhi al-wazīru dandānu min akhbāri al-mutaqaddimīna mina al-mulūki wa-al-mutayyamīna
sentences.l: And when Ḍawʾ al-Makān heard the words of the vizier Dandān, his heart hung on what he had promised him, and there remained to him no occupation except with the awaiting of the coming of the night, for the sake that he might hear what the vizier Dandān would tell of the reports of the former-ones of the kings and the love-enslaved.
sentences.i: When Ḍawʾ al-Makān heard the vizier Dandān’s words, his heart was set on what he had been promised, and he could think of nothing but waiting for night to come, to hear what the vizier Dandān would tell of the kings and lovers of old.
sentences.n: taʿallaqa qalbuhu bi-, “his heart clung to”: the bi- gives what the heart is fixed on; waʿadahu bihi, “promised him (it)”, takes bi- for the thing promised.

sentences.t: فَمَا صَدَّقَ أَنَّ اللَّيْلَ أَقْبَلَ حَتَّى أَمَرَ بِإِيقَادِ الشُّمُوعِ وَالْقَنَادِيلِ وَإِحْضَارِ مَا يَحْتَاجُونَ إِلَيْهِ مِنَ الْأَكْلِ وَالشُّرْبِ وَآلَاتِ الْبَخُورِ
sentences.tr: fa-mā ṣaddaqa anna al-layla aqbala ḥattā amara bi-īqādi al-shumūʿi wa-al-qanādīli wa-iḥḍāri mā yaḥtājūna ilayhi mina al-akli wa-al-shurbi wa-ālāti al-bakhūri
sentences.l: And he hardly believed that the night had come-on before he ordered the kindling of the candles and the lamps, and the bringing of what they would need of the eating and the drinking and the implements of the incense.
sentences.i: No sooner had night come on than he ordered the candles and lamps lit, and everything brought that they would need of food and drink and censers.
sentences.n: fa-mā ṣaddaqa anna … ḥattā, literally “he did not believe that … until”, is a later idiom for “no sooner … than”: he could scarcely believe night had come before he was giving orders.

sentences.t: فَأَحْضَرُوا لَهُ جَمِيعَ ذَلِكَ ثُمَّ أَرْسَلَ إِلَى الْوَزِيرِ دَنْدَانَ فَحَضَرَ وَأَرْسَلَ إِلَى بَهْرَامَ وَرُسْتُمَ وَتُرْكَاشَ وَالْحَاجِبِ الْكَبِيرِ فَحَضَرُوا
sentences.tr: fa-aḥḍarū lahu jamīʿa dhālika thumma arsala ilā al-wazīri dandāna fa-ḥaḍara wa-arsala ilā bahrāma wa-rustuma wa-turkāsha wa-al-ḥājibi al-kabīri fa-ḥaḍarū
sentences.l: And they brought to him all of that; then he sent to the vizier Dandān, and he came; and he sent to Bahrām and Rustam and Turkāsh and the chamberlain the great, and they came.
sentences.i: They brought him all of it; then he sent for the vizier Dandān, who came, and sent for Bahrām, Rustam, Turkāsh and the Great Chamberlain, and they came.
sentences.n: arsala ilā, “sent to”, is “sent for” someone. The Great Chamberlain is Nuzhat al-Zamān’s husband.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا حَضَرَ جَمِيعُهُمْ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ الْتَفَتَ إِلَى الْوَزِيرِ دَنْدَانَ وَقَالَ لَهُ اعْلَمْ أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ أَنَّ اللَّيْلَ قَدْ أَقْبَلَ وَسَدَلَ جَلَابِيبَهُ عَلَيْنَا وَأَسْبَلَ وَنُرِيدُ أَنْ تَحْكِىَ لَنَا مَا وَعَدْتَنَا بِهِ مِنَ الْحِكَايَاتِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ḥaḍara jamīʿuhum bayna yadayhi iltafata ilā al-wazīri dandāna wa-qāla lahu iʿlam ayyuhā al-wazīru anna al-layla qad aqbala wa-sadala jalābībahu ʿalaynā wa-asbala wa-nurīdu an taḥkiya lanā mā waʿadtanā bihi mina al-ḥikāyāti
sentences.l: And when all of them were present between his two hands, he turned to the vizier Dandān and said to him: Know, O vizier, that the night has come-on, and has drawn its mantles down over us and let (them) fall; and we wish that you tell us what you promised us of the tales.
sentences.i: When they were all before him he turned to the vizier Dandān and said, “Know, O vizier, that night has come and drawn its cloaks down over us; we would have you tell us the tales you promised.”
sentences.n: bayna yadayhi, “between his two hands”, is “in his presence”. Rhymed prose: aqbala / asbala. jalābīb are long outer cloaks; night lets them fall over the world. taḥkī is printed with ى for ي.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْوَزِيرُ حُبًّا وَكَرَامَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-wazīru ḥubban wa-karāmatan
sentences.l: And the vizier said: With love and honour.
sentences.i: “Gladly, and with all my heart,” said the vizier.
sentences.n: ḥubban wa-karāmatan, “out of love and honour”, the fixed reply of glad consent.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
